What happens to shares when someone dies in Australia?

By the Afterkeep research team · Reviewed on 23 Nov 2026

Shares stay in the deceased person's name until the estate deals with them. If they're CHESS-sponsored (a HIN starting with X), the sponsoring broker handles it. If they're issuer-sponsored (an SRN), contact the company's share registry, such as Computershare or MUFG Corporate Markets. Shares can be transmitted into the executor's name or transferred straight to beneficiaries; there's no need to transmit first. For a sole holding of an Australian resident, Computershare accepts a death certificate, the will and a Small Estate Indemnity form for holdings worth up to A$50,000. Above that it needs probate. A surviving joint holder uses a separate form.

Key facts

  • CHESS (HIN starts with X): go through the broker
  • Computershare: up to A$50,000 per holding, will + death certificate + indemnity
  • Over A$50,000: probate or letters of administration
  • Registries don't sell shares; use a broker

What are the steps?

  1. Find the holdings: look for holding statements, dividend statements and emails. Note each company, the SRN (10 digits, starting with I) or HIN, and the name and address exactly as registered.
  2. CHESS-sponsored holdings (HIN starts with X): contact the sponsoring broker. Both Computershare and MUFG say the broker deals with the estate for these.
  3. Issuer-sponsored holdings: contact the registry named on the statement. MUFG offers an online questionnaire that lists the forms and documents your situation needs.
  4. Work out what each holding is worth. Computershare's Australian checklist sets the paperwork by value: up to A$50,000 with a will, a certified death certificate, the will and a 'Small Estate Indemnity' form (or probate). Over A$50,000, probate. With no will: up to A$50,000, the death certificate and an 'Intestacy Request and Indemnity' form (or letters of administration); over that, letters of administration.
  5. Use a registry death certificate. MUFG says a medical death certificate isn't enough; it needs the certificate issued by Births, Deaths and Marriages.
  6. Add any extra forms that apply. Computershare asks for a 'Confirmation of the Deceased's Name' form if the register name differs from the legal documents, and a 'Section 1071B Statement' if probate is granted in a different state from where the shares are registered. For South Australian probate, get a Section 121A Registrar's Certificate of Disclosure.
  7. Choose the outcome: a 'Transmission Application' puts the shares in the executor's name for later distribution; a 'Standard Transfer' moves them straight to beneficiaries or buyers. Registries don't sell shares; Computershare says to contact a broker to sell.
  8. Send it properly. Computershare needs a separate form for each holding, original forms with ink signatures (no copies, fax or email) and originally certified copies of legal documents, not the originals. MUFG accepts completed forms by email or post.
  9. Check for old dividends or shares already handed to ASIC as unclaimed money; see our unclaimed money guide.

Frequently asked questions

What happens to shares when someone dies in Australia?

They stay in the deceased's name until the executor or administrator has them transmitted into the executor's name, transferred to beneficiaries, or sold through a broker. CHESS-sponsored shares go through the sponsoring broker; issuer-sponsored shares go through the company's share registry.

Do you need probate to transfer shares?

Not always. Computershare's Australian checklist accepts a certified death certificate, the will and a Small Estate Indemnity form where a holding is worth up to A$50,000. Above A$50,000 it needs Australian probate (or letters of administration if there's no will).

What's the difference between transmission and transfer?

MUFG explains that transmission moves shares from the deceased's name into the executor's name as trustee for the estate. Transfer moves them to the final beneficiaries, either from the executor or directly from the deceased. You can often transfer directly without transmitting first.

How do I know if shares are CHESS or issuer sponsored?

Check the holding statement. A HIN beginning with X means CHESS-sponsored, so contact the broker. An issuer-sponsored holding has an SRN, which Computershare describes as a 10-digit number starting with I.

Can shares be registered in the name of an estate or a child?

Not on Computershare's Standard Transfer. It says securities can't be registered in the name of a trust, a super fund, a minor, an estate or a deceased person, and a maximum of three holders can be registered.

What if the shares were held jointly?

Computershare's checklist doesn't cover joint holdings; it points to its 'Request to Register Surviving Securityholder(s)' form. MUFG lists 'transmit to surviving joint holder(s)' as one of the options.
